newsitem.title: USA: Closing landfill may cut NYC landfill costs - Hevesi.
newsitem.headline: Closing landfill may cut NYC landfill costs - Hevesi.

text.p: The New York City Comptroller Alan Hevesi on Wednesday estimated that the amount the city spends on recycling will fall once the Fresh Kills landfill, the world's largest, on Staten Island is closed.
The comptroller urged the Giuliani Administration, which has promised to close the landfill, to expand the recycling program and comply with a court order requiring it to recyle 4,250 tons a day.

"Recycling has been attacked as being too expensive, but that view is short-sighted," Hevesi said in prepared remarks t was important for the city to avoid being totally dependent on exporting its garbage.

The comptroller estimated that in 2002, when Fresh Kills is scheduled to be closed, as required by state law, the net cost of recycling will vary between a cost of $67 a ton and a savings of $32 a ton.

Increased efficiency, a moderate market for recyclables and average costs for exporting could help push the net cost could down to $19 a ton. New York City now spends an additional $75 a ton to recycle garbage, Hevesi said.

He added that while the Giuliani Administration in the November budget modification approved spending $6 million more on recycling, about $4 million of that sum will pay for higher costs, like paying recyclers to take paper because the newsprint prices have fallen, not restoring services.
